clue.text: Bobby out to slow down traffic?

definitions.text: Bobby out to slow down traffic?

parts.words: Bobby out to slow down traffic?
parts.note: a bobby is a British policeman; a hump across the road is nicknamed a sleeping policeman, a bobby who is out cold

explanation.surface: A police officer is sent out on the street to calm the traffic.
explanation.walkthrough: BOBBY is British slang for a police officer; the road hump is known in Britain as a 'sleeping policeman', so 'out' means asleep rather than on patrol.
explanation.definitionFit: A raised hump across a road, nicknamed a sleeping policeman, forces drivers to slow.

clue.text: Exercises aged uncle — like oysters?

parts.note: PE is physical education, school exercises
Edward Lear's poem begins 'O my aged Uncle Arly'

explanation.surface: An elderly relative is put through gym routines, with a question about shellfish.
explanation.walkthrough: Uncle Arly is the subject of an Edward Lear nonsense poem, which opens 'O my aged Uncle Arly'.
explanation.definitionFit: Oysters produce pearls, so something resembling or containing pearls can be called pearly.

clue.text: In this sergeant takes up a way out

indicators.note: in a down clue, taking letters up means reading them from the bottom, backwards
the letters sit inside the words this sergeant, running across the gap between them

explanation.surface: A sergeant picks out an exit route.
explanation.walkthrough: 'In' points to letters within 'this sergeant' (SSERGE), and 'takes up' turns them round in this down entry.
explanation.definitionFit: An egress is an exit, the route by which one leaves a place.

clue.text: Artist drinking a little rich soup

indicators.note: one thing drinking another takes it inside, so the painter's name holds the letter

parts.note: Hieronymus Bosch, the Dutch painter

indicators.note: only a small part of the word rich is used, its opening letter

explanation.surface: A painter sips a small amount of a rich soup.
explanation.walkthrough: 'drinking' puts R, the first letter of 'rich' (from 'a little'), inside BOSCH.
explanation.definitionFit: Borsch is the beetroot broth of Eastern Europe, a kind of soup.

clue.text: 40-60 thickening, giving 400-1500?

definitions.meaning: the waistline thickening that comes with the years between forty and sixty
the medieval period, roughly AD 400 to 1500, spread out across centuries

explanation.surface: Two sets of numbers are compared, one of ages and one of dates.
explanation.walkthrough: The first reading is the paunch of later life; the second takes the Middle Ages, AD 400-1500, as a stretch of time spread out.
explanation.definitionFit: Weight gained round the waist in the forties and fifties has this idiomatic name, while the medieval era covers those dates.

clue.text: Instrument of ready fit

parts.note: set means ready, as in 'all set'
to square with something is to fit or agree with it

explanation.surface: A tool described as ready and suitable.
explanation.definitionFit: A set square is a triangular drawing tool used by draughtsmen for right angles.

clue.text: Even great footballer can do no more than this

definitions.text: can do no more than this

parts.note: level means even or flat
George Best, the Northern Ireland and Manchester United star

explanation.surface: Even a star player has limits to what he can achieve.
explanation.walkthrough: George Best was a celebrated Northern Ireland footballer of the 1960s.
explanation.definitionFit: One's level best is the utmost effort possible, beyond which nothing more can be done.

clue.text: Recovered, say, no longer under stress

definitions.note: recovered is an example of a verb form, so 'say' marks an instance

parts.note: something past is over, no longer the case
tense means strained or under stress

explanation.surface: Someone has got better and is no longer anxious.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Recovered' looks like the state of a patient, but it is offered as a grammatical example.
explanation.definitionFit: Recovered is a verb in its preterite form, an example of this grammatical category.

clue.text: It paid Catalan electronic group to smash generator

indicators.note: the pieces break into the father's word, landing between its letters

parts.note: a father generates offspring; PA is father
a set is a group

explanation.surface: A Catalan electronic band wrecks a power generator, which somebody paid for.
explanation.walkthrough: 'to smash' puts the electronic group inside the generator. 'Generator' looks like machinery but is a begetter, a father, and the definition uses the past tense because the coin was replaced by the euro.
explanation.definitionFit: Spain's currency before the euro, so it was the money a Catalan paid with.

clue.text: Smuggling divers are adrift

indicators.note: divers is an old word for various or assorted, so the letters that follow are put into a different order

explanation.surface: Underwater smugglers have lost their bearings at sea.
explanation.walkthrough: 'divers' looks like swimmers but is the archaic adjective meaning various, signalling the anagram. In the eighteenth century this phrase was a euphemism for smuggling.
explanation.definitionFit: An old euphemism for running contraband past customs, now used of ethical commerce.

clue.text: So Telegraph's quoted verbatim, it's agreed

parts.note: as can mean so, in the sense of 'just as'
something telegraphed has been sent; 'quoted verbatim' points to the phrase used of a message reproduced exactly as it was sent

explanation.surface: A newspaper report is quoted word for word, and everyone agrees.
explanation.walkthrough: 'quoted verbatim' hints that the two pieces together form the phrase used for a telegram reproduced unchanged.
explanation.definitionFit: Assent is agreement or consent, the state when something is agreed.

clue.text: Squeak: 'Time, gentlemen, please!'?

definitions.meaning: a narrow squeak is a near miss
the cry of a British pub landlord announcing closing time

explanation.surface: A pub's closing announcement.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Time, gentlemen, please!' is what a British publican calls at closing time.
explanation.definitionFit: A near miss is a narrow squeak; a landlord's closing-time shout is literally a call to close.

clue.text: What might be put up for sale — of ales?

definitions.text: What might be put up for sale — of ales?

parts.words: What might be put up for sale — of ales?
parts.note: secondhand odds and ends offered at a charity sale; and a muddle of the letters of ales makes sale

explanation.surface: Wondering what goods might be offered at a sale of beers.
explanation.walkthrough: The word describes both the goods at a charity sale and a mixing-up, which turns the letters of 'ales' into 'sale'.
explanation.definitionFit: Assorted secondhand items donated for a charity bazaar go by this name, and the word also means a muddle.

clue.text: Uncultured individual, being quite big and fit, turns in

parts.note: esse is Latin for 'to be', used for existence or being

indicators.note: the reversed piece goes inside the size label

parts.note: XL is extra large on clothes labels

indicators.note: the word for fit turns round, read from its end

parts.note: to rig is to fit out or equip

explanation.surface: A boorish person who is rather large and healthy turns up.
explanation.walkthrough: 'turns' reverses the word for fit and 'in' sets it inside the size label. An Essex girl is a British stereotype of a brash, unsophisticated young woman from the county east of London.
explanation.definitionFit: A stock British jibe for a supposedly vulgar, unrefined woman, here labelled an uncultured person.

clue.text: More security provided for Spooner's door, and feature of it?

indicators.note: Dr Spooner swapped the opening sounds of words, so the starts of the two words trade places

parts.note: better means more, as in better than half
locks provide security

explanation.surface: A householder wants stronger security for the front door.
explanation.walkthrough: Better locks for a door, with the first sounds swapped, becomes a slot that is a feature of that door.
explanation.definitionFit: A slot in a front door for post is a common feature of it.

clue.text: Here one's putting the hours in?

definitions.text: Here one's putting the hours in?

parts.words: Here one's putting the hours in?
parts.note: a lawn game in which players putt from points marked round a circle like the numbers on a dial

explanation.surface: A place where somebody works long shifts.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Putting' is golf putting, not placing, and the hours are the twelve positions round the lawn.
explanation.definitionFit: A lawn putting game played from twelve positions laid out like a dial's numerals.

clue.text: Pastoral song To a Skylark?

indicators.note: to skylark is to frolic or play about, so these letters are playfully rearranged

explanation.surface: Shelley's poem 'To a Skylark' as a song of the countryside.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Skylark' looks like the bird of the poem title but is a verb, to fool around. An oat is a shepherd's pipe, hence a pastoral song in poetry.
explanation.definitionFit: In poetic usage an oaten pipe stands for rustic shepherd music, a literary sense of the word.

clue.text: The heavyweight of Chinese food, so I've heard

indicators.note: the words say the dumpling's name as it is spoken, matching the sound of the entry

parts.note: a wonton is a Chinese dumpling

explanation.surface: The heftiest item in a Chinese meal, according to rumour.
explanation.definitionFit: Something weighing a full imperial unit of 2240 pounds is a heavyweight indeed.

clue.text: See 17
Image in one piece, filmgoer's lesson not?

indicators.note: the clue asks for something that is not the filmgoer's lesson as written, so those letters are rearranged

explanation.surface: A cinema-goer's takeaway, framed as a negative question.
explanation.walkthrough: The anagram of FILMGOERS plus LESSON is signalled by 'not?'. To come up smelling of roses is to emerge with reputation intact.
explanation.definitionFit: The idiom describes an untarnished reputation, a public image that survives unscathed.

clue.text: In the end, Shakespeare's flat

indicators.note: the letters lie within the words the end, straddling the gap

explanation.surface: At the close, the playwright is level.
explanation.walkthrough: 'In the end' looks like a phrase meaning finally, but it signals letters inside 'the end'.
explanation.definitionFit: The poetic contraction of even, meaning level, is common in Elizabethan verse.

clue.text: Tempt fate losing weight, see, losing round figure

indicators.note: the word fate gives up the letters standing for body weight

parts.note: losing weight means shedding fat

indicators.note: the word for see drops the round numeral

parts.note: to see something is to notice it
O, the round numeral zero

explanation.surface: Taking a risk by dieting and giving up shape.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Tempt fate' looks like one phrase, but only 'Tempt' defines; 'fate' is fodder, and 'weight' is the fat a dieter loses.
explanation.definitionFit: To lure or seduce someone into doing something is to tempt them.

clue.text: Henry's working with Telegraph's integrity

parts.note: H is the symbol for the henry, the unit of inductance
on means working, as a machine that is on
the newspaper speaking of itself would say our

explanation.surface: A man called Henry works for the newspaper and has principles.
explanation.walkthrough: The clue appeared in the Telegraph, so 'Telegraph's' means belonging to us: OUR.
explanation.definitionFit: Honour is moral uprightness and adherence to principle, a synonym for integrity.

clue.text: One amongst basics observed by you and me? You can count on it

indicators.note: the group of you and me follows on, watching from behind
the single letter goes among the letters of the basics

parts.note: the ABC of something is its basics
A means one
us is you and me

explanation.surface: One thing among the fundamentals that we notice is reliable.
explanation.walkthrough: 'You can count on it' sounds like a promise of reliability but means a counting frame.
explanation.definitionFit: A frame with beads on wires, used to count and calculate.

clue.text: Power to cross a range of mountains

indicators.note: the letter for power cuts across the phrase, landing inside it

parts.note: a range is a line or row

explanation.surface: Energy is needed to get across a mountain range.
explanation.walkthrough: 'range' looks like the mountains but is a line; 'to cross' puts P inside A LINE.
explanation.definitionFit: The word describes things relating to high mountains, especially the Alps.

clue.text: Court summons William Bird

parts.note: to spoon is an old word for courting or canoodling
Bill is short for William

explanation.surface: A court issues a summons to a man named William Bird.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Court' looks like a law court but is the verb, to woo, as is old-fashioned 'spoon'.
explanation.definitionFit: A long-legged wading bird with a flat, broad bill like a spoon.

clue.text: Form of rock music or Motown establishment?

definitions.meaning: a raw, amateur style of rock played in rehearsal spaces at home
Motown is taken literally as motor town, where a car workshop would be found

explanation.surface: A choice between a genre and a famous record label.
explanation.walkthrough: Motown is the Detroit record label, but read as motor town it suggests a workshop for cars.
explanation.definitionFit: A rough rock style and a car repair shop share this word.

clue.text: Gold glimpsed in tree is a flower

indicators.note: the gold is seen within the tree, so it goes inside

parts.note: the beech is a tree
or is gold in heraldry

explanation.surface: A golden glint in a tree turns out to be a bloom.
explanation.definitionFit: A wild orchid whose bloom resembles a bee, a plant in flower.

clue.text: Grub to put back in part

indicators.note: the turned word goes inside the word for part

parts.note: a role is a part in a play

indicators.note: the little word to is put back to front

explanation.surface: Putting a piece back where it belongs.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Grub' looks like food but is the verb, to dig about; 'put back' gives OT, set 'in' ROLE.
explanation.definitionFit: To rootle is to rummage or dig about, as a pig does with its snout.

clue.text: A covering letter's enclosed for me?

indicators.note: the letter's name holds the covering inside it

parts.note: dee is the spelt-out name of the letter D
a dress is a covering for the body

explanation.surface: Someone asks whether a covering letter in the envelope is meant for them.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Covering letter' looks like one thing, a note sent with documents, but it splits in two; 'letter's' is the spelt-out name of a letter, and 'for me?' is what the recipient asks.
explanation.definitionFit: The recipient named on an envelope, the person to whom mail is directed.
